As someone who's been doing internet roleplay since 1998 or thereabouts, I will tell you that a lot of the same pitfalls that happen in person will happen online. People can be just as flaky, sometimes moreso, online as well as they are in person.

Friend ran a game, and to bolster our playerbase, I invited a friend of mine, a veteran roleplayer. Originally just to consult on some of the game's subject matter, as she was already knowledgeable about where we were playing. But then we invited her to play, and She was super excited to participate and then, when the game started, we'd have maybe 20% of her attention. Either she'd be too busy with something else to do much more than tag along with the other characters, or she'd start playing and a quarter of the way in she'd just disappear. Fortunately, there were enough of the rest of us, that we were able to play on through without her most days.

So, I'd say one lesson is to be flexible. Either be prepared to just gloss over the presence/non-presence of players, be ready to be dynamic about your party, or build it in to your setting, some way to account for a shifting cast. That or be prepared to have a lot of off-days. Though, as you've already alluded to, that's a more pressing issue for Synchronous means of play.

Personally, Synchronous forms are my preferred means of play. maybe its just how ADD i am, but I don't like big solitary posts that are slowly responded to. I need to be able to play off of others, to have an actual conversation rather than just monologue at each other. I need to be able to react, and respond and inspire and provoke in near-real-time. Sometimes all I have to say is a sentence, or all I have to do is a small gesture, and forum play is poorly suited to that.

As such, I personally have a strong preference for realtime chat or virtual tabletops for play. in the above example we used Roll20 for our game. Never touched a microphone for it either, though I've a strong inclination to use them next time I do a game on there, just for OOC chatter, to keep people involved in the game and active.
